topics.name: Energy Fields
topics.description: Explore wave-particle duality, fields, and the forces that shape reality.

questions.question: What is a field in physics?
options: A value or quantity spread across space and time
A tiny hard ball inside atoms
questions.explanation: A field is a physical quantity that has a value at every point in space and time. Examples include gravitational, electric, and magnetic fields.

questions.question: Which field is responsible for electricity and magnetism?
questions.explanation: The electromagnetic field explains light, electricity, magnetism, radio waves, and X-rays. It is one of the four fundamental forces.

questions.question: What does the Higgs field give to particles?
questions.explanation: The Higgs field permeates all of space. When particles interact with it, they acquire mass. The Higgs boson was confirmed at CERN in 2012.

questions.question: Which fundamental force has infinite range?
questions.explanation: Both gravity and electromagnetism have infinite range. Gravity dominates at large scales because it is always attractive and acts on all mass-energy.

questions.question: What particle carries the electromagnetic force?
questions.explanation: The photon is the force-carrying particle of the electromagnetic field. It is massless and always travels at the speed of light.

questions.question: What is a gravitational field?
options: A region where a mass experiences gravitational force
The area inside a black hole
The spin of electrons around the nucleus
questions.explanation: A gravitational field is a region of space where a mass experiences gravitational force. Described by Einstein's general relativity as curvature of spacetime.

questions.question: What is a quantum field?
options: A field only visible under a microscope
A field that is quantized into discrete particles
A field inside an atom only
questions.explanation: In quantum field theory, every fundamental particle is an excitation (vibration) of an underlying quantum field that permeates all of space.

questions.question: Which field is associated with the W and Z bosons?
questions.explanation: The W and Z bosons carry the weak nuclear force, responsible for radioactive beta decay. They are about 80-91 times heavier than a proton.

questions.question: How does gravity compare to electromagnetism in strength?
questions.explanation: Gravity is about 10^36 times weaker than electromagnetism. Yet gravity dominates at cosmic scales because it cannot be shielded or cancelled.

questions.question: What did CERN confirm in 2012?
questions.explanation: The Higgs boson was confirmed at CERN's Large Hadron Collider in July 2012, completing the Standard Model and confirming the mass-giving Higgs field.

topics.name: Quarks & Hadrons
topics.description: Explore the subatomic world of quarks, gluons, and the strong nuclear force.

questions.question: Which fundamental particle acts as the mediator of the strong nuclear force, binding quarks together within protons and neutrons?
questions.explanation: Gluons are the force-carrying particles of the strong nuclear force (QCD). They bind quarks together and carry color charge themselves, unlike photons which are chargeless.

questions.question: How many quark flavors exist in the Standard Model?
questions.explanation: There are 6 quark flavors: up, down, charm, strange, top, and bottom. They come in three generations of increasing mass.

questions.question: What are the three quarks inside a proton?
options: Two up quarks and one down quark
Two down quarks and one up quark
One up and two strange quarks
questions.explanation: A proton consists of two up quarks (+2/3 each) and one down quark (-1/3), giving a total charge of +1. Quarks are held by gluons via the strong force.

questions.question: What is quark confinement?
options: Quarks are found only in stars
Quarks cannot exist in isolation — they always form hadrons
Quarks are confined to the nucleus only
questions.explanation: Quark confinement means quarks are never found alone. Trying to separate them creates new quark-antiquark pairs instead. They always bind into hadrons.

questions.question: What is a meson?
options: A particle made of a quark and an antiquark
questions.explanation: A meson is a hadron made of one quark and one antiquark. Pions and kaons are common examples. Mesons are unstable and decay quickly.

questions.question: How many 'colors' can a quark carry?
questions.explanation: Quarks carry one of three color charges: red, green, or blue. This is Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). 'Color' is a metaphor — not actual visible color.

questions.question: What is the charge of a down quark?
questions.explanation: The down quark has a charge of -1/3. Two up quarks (+2/3 each) plus one down quark (-1/3) produce the proton's total charge of +1.

questions.question: Which quark is the heaviest?
questions.explanation: The top quark is the heaviest at ~173 GeV/c² — roughly as massive as an entire tungsten atom. It decays before it can form hadrons.

questions.question: What is a baryon?
questions.explanation: A baryon is a hadron made of three quarks. Protons and neutrons are the most common baryons. Baryons are subject to baryon number conservation.

questions.question: What does QCD stand for?
questions.explanation: QCD — Quantum Chromodynamics — is the theory describing the strong interaction between quarks via gluons. 'Chromo' refers to the color charge carried by quarks.
